title: Genesis 3. The Cup Drained.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 3. The Cup Drained.
The serpent begins by questioning God's word.
Then he contradicts it.
"Did God really say?
Not an argument.
A question.
The first crack in the Cup is not a blow,
it is a question about whether the Cup is trustworthy.
The serpent is more subtle than any creature God made.
He does not attack the boundary.
He reinterprets it.
He tells the woman: You will not die.
God knows that when you eat, your eyes will be opened,
and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.
The woman sees.
The tree is good for food.
It is a delight to the eyes.
It is to be desired to make one wise.
She takes.
She eats.
She gives to her husband, who is with her.
He eats.
Everything until now has been gift, light, life, breath, garden, companion.
The rhythm of six days was: God speaks, it happens, God sees,
God names, God gives.
Now man reaches for what was not given.
The first act of grabbing instead of receiving.
The Cup does not overflow, it drains.
Eyes are opened.
But what they see is themselves.
They know that they are naked.
The transparency of chapter two, naked and not ashamed, is gone.
Shame enters where there was none.
They sew fig leaves together.
They hear the sound of God walking in the garden in the cool of the day,
and they hide.
The Cup is no longer transparent.
It is covered.
God calls: "Where are you?
Not because He does not know.
Because the relationship has changed.
The man who was naked and unashamed now hides among the trees.
God asks: Who told you that you were naked?
Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?
And the man answers: The woman You gave me,
she gave me fruit, and I ate.
The woman answers: The serpent deceived me, and I ate.
Neither stands.
Neither carries what they have done.
The Cup that was shared in chapter two now splits,
each hand pointing away from itself.
The man blames the gift.
The woman blames the deceiver.
The vessel that was made for communion turns to accusation.
God speaks to the serpent first.
Cursed above all livestock, above every beast of the field.
On your belly you shall go.
Dust you shall eat all the days of your life.
Then, inside the curse,
a word that does not yet have its full shape:
I will put hostility between you and the woman,
between your offspring and her offspring.
He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.
The Cup is drained.
But inside the draining,
something is planted that has not yet been named.
A wound is promised to the one who caused the wound.
The seed of the woman has not yet appeared.
But the hostility between her offspring and the serpent has been declared.
What this means will not become clear for a very long time.
To the woman: pain in childbirth multiplied.
Desire toward her husband.
He shall rule over her.
To the man: the ground is cursed because of you.
Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread,
until you return to the ground.
For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.
The vessel that was dust receiving breath is told: you are dust,
and to dust you shall return.
The breath remains.
But the body's end is now spoken.
What was given in chapter two is not taken back,
but its frame has changed.
The Cup that held life without death now holds life that ends.
The man names his wife Eve,
because she was the mother of all the living.
Then God makes garments of skin and clothes them.
God makes garments of skin and clothes them.
The text does not say how the skins were obtained,
what creature they came from,
or whether this scene is narrating a death.
The fig leaves were their own attempt to cover themselves, self-made,
sewn in shame.
God does not leave them in their own covering.
He clothes them with what they did not make for themselves.
The Cup is empty, but God does not leave them uncovered.
Then God says: Behold, the man has become like one of Us,
knowing good and evil.
Now lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat and live forever,
The sentence does not finish.
But the action does.
He sends them out.
He drives the man out of the garden of Eden,
to work the ground from which he was taken.
At the east of Eden He places cherubim,
and a flaming sword that turned every direction,
to guard the way to the tree of life.
The Cup is not destroyed.
It is closed.
The way back is preserved, but protected.
The tree of life still stands.
The garden still exists.
But the way is no longer open.
Something has come between man and what he was made to receive.
What began in rest now moves in sweat and thorns and dust.
What was transparent is now covered.
What was shared is now divided.
What was given freely has been grabbed.
And the question asked in the garden, "Where are you?",
has not yet been answered.
